title: cache-coordination-lease-allocator-spec
body:
Summary:
This note proposes a lightweight, distributed lease-based allocator for our KV cache to reduce cross-shard races, lower fragmentation, and provide a clear fast-path for tenant-local mutations. The approach is intentionally coordination-minimal (no full raft cluster per cache) but borrows lease semantics (ownership window, renewals, and explicit handoff) to make eviction and compaction safer across replicas and threads.

Goals:
- Prevent duplicated reclamation work and wrong-path evictions during heavy multi-tenant churn.
- Bound client-visible tail latency by making eviction decisions predictable.
- Enable low-cost compaction windows that operate without global stop-the-world pauses.
- Reduce long-term fragmentation by colocating slots under stable leases for hot prefixes.

Key concepts:
- Microshard: small namespace unit (e.g., prefix hash range or tenant bucket). Each microshard manages local metadata and a lease owner id.
- Lease: short-lived ownership token (default 200ms) granted to a worker thread/process that intends to mutate placement (evict/insert/compact) for that microshard.
- Lease coordinator: lightweight, in-process or RPC-backed table that grants/renews leases. No consensus required—leases are best-effort with epoch counters.
- Slot groups / pools: memory separated into hot/warm/cold pools with different compaction heuristics and eviction costs.

Allocator workflow (fast path):
1) Request arrives for a key in microshard S. Local worker attempts to acquire microshard lease from local coordinator cache (atomic CAS against epoch).
2) If lease acquired and slot available in hot/warm pool, mutate in-place (update KV headers, bump hotness).
3) If insertion requires allocation and hot pool full, allocator attempts bounded local spill into warm pool. If warm full, mark candidate for eviction and schedule asynchronous eviction under the same lease.
4) Lease renewals: hot write paths can renew lease cheaply (single-word CAS) to extend ownership up to a capped limit.

Slow path (contention or lost lease):
- If lease cannot be obtained within a short window (~1-2ms), worker uses safe-read-only path: serve reads, enqueues write to background mutator, and returns a transient error or backpressure signal to the client depending on policy. Background mutator will attempt to acquire lease and apply changes.

Eviction & compaction semantics:
- Eviction decision uses combined score = occupancy-quantile * tenant-weight * recency-decay. Microshard lease ensures only one actor performs eviction for that microshard in a lease interval.
- Compact candidates are groups of fragmented slots inside a pool. Compaction is performed by atomic swap: preallocate destination region, copy live entries, update pointer table under the microshard lease, and then free source slab. This avoids intermediate inconsistent reads.
- To avoid long GC pauses, compaction work is chunked and idempotent: each chunk has a seqno and can be resumed.

Memory pools and fragmentation handling:
- Hot pool: small, fast-alloc slabs optimized for short-lived KV with high update rate. Tight LRU + lease locality expected.
- Warm pool: larger slabs, used for spill and semi-stable prefixes. Coalescing of adjacent small free slots is allowed only during compaction windows to bound allocation latency.
- Cold pool: large persistent slabs, used for long-tail items; freed via background batch reclamation to avoid fragmentation storms.
- Fragmentation metrics to record per-pool: free-run-length histogram, external-fragmentation-ratio, average-slot-waste, compaction-score. These are exposed per-microshard for telemetry and SLIs.

Observability and signals:
- Expose per-microshard lease contention rate, avg lease hold time, lease renew/fail counts, compaction-chunk-duration, and eviction-error-rate.
- Alert if global free-run-length 95p exceeds threshold OR average compaction backpressure > 60s.

Safety and failure modes:
- Lease expiry semantics: if holder dies, lease naturally expires and a subsequent actor may acquire after epoch increment. To mitigate split-brain on immediate failover, we use monotonic epoch counters persisted in memtable for microshard metadata.
- Crash during compaction: since updates to pointer table are atomic under lease and copy is to preallocated destination, readers either see old or new region. A background reaper will reclaim abandoned preallocs after lease epochs lapse.

Experimentation plan:
- Phase 0: unit tests + microbench: simulate 1k microshards, 128B avg entry, bursty writes to 10% tenants. Measure tail latency, eviction throughput, and fragmentation score vs baseline.
- Phase 1: small fleet A/B deploy in non-critical region; enable lease allocator for 10% traffic. Track degraded request rate (>0.1%) and compaction ops.
- Phase 2: tune lease durations, spill thresholds, and compaction chunk sizes.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Lease duration tuning: shorter reduces contention but increases churn and renew overhead. Need workload characterization by tenant.
- Coordination backend: in-process only vs lightweight RPC for cross-host microshard ownership (for Dedicated/Private). Trade memory overhead vs correctness.
- Tenant fairness: should high-paying tenants get stronger lease guarantees? (prefer to expose as configurable policy rather than hard-coded)

Next steps / TODOs:
- Prototype in serving-runtime branch (PR link above) with feature flag.
- Build microshard simulator that models tenant burst patterns and measures fragmentation growth.
- Add telemetry dashboards and heatmap for microshard compaction pressure.
- Write operator playbook: emergency compaction, manual lease steal command, safe rollback steps.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an exploratory design targeted at reducing multi-actor interference and improving long-term fragmentation without central consensus. Comments welcome on lease sizing heuristics and whether we should fold this into existing slot allocator interfaces or keep as separate layer.

End.
